abstract: <jats:p>A moderately halophilic, aerobic, motile, Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium (strain LV4<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>) was isolated from saline soil around the lake Laguna Verde in the Bolivian Andes. The organism is a heterotroph, able to utilize various carbohydrates as a carbon source. It showed tryptophan deaminase, oxidase and catalase activity, but was unable to produce indole or H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>S; nitrate was not reduced. The G+C content of the genomic DNA was 56·1 mol%. The pH range for growth was 5–10, temperature range was 0–45 °C and the range of NaCl concentrations was 0–25 % (w/v). On the basis of 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis, strain LV4<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> was found to be closely related to <jats:italic>Chromohalobacter canadensis</jats:italic> DSM 6769<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> and <jats:italic>Pseudomonas beijerinckii</jats:italic> DSM 7218<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>; however, its DNA–DNA relatedness with these type strains was low. Strain LV4<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> resembled other <jats:italic>Chromohalobacter</jats:italic> species with respect to various physiological, biochemical and nutritional characteristics but also exhibited differences. Thus, a novel species, <jats:italic>Chromohalobacter sarecensis</jats:italic> sp. nov., is proposed, with LV4<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> (=CCUG 47987<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>=ATCC BAA-761<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>) as the type strain.</jats:p>

                  <jats:italic>Halomonas boliviensis</jats:italic> sp. nov. is proposed for two moderately halophilic, psychrophilic, alkalitolerant bacteria, LC1<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> (=DSM 15516<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>=ATCC BAA-759<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>) and LC2 (=DSM 15517=ATCC BAA-760), both of which were isolated from a soil sample around the lake Laguna Colorada, located at 4300 m above sea level in the south-west region of Bolivia. The organisms reduce nitrate and show tryptophan deaminase activity. The genomic DNA G+C contents were 51·4 mol% for isolate LC1<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> and 52·6 mol% for isolate LC2. Based on 16S rDNA sequence analysis, isolates LC1<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> and LC2 were identified as members of the genus <jats:italic>Halomonas</jats:italic> and clustered closely with <jats:italic>Halomonas variabilis</jats:italic> DSM 3051<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> and <jats:italic>Halomonas meridiana</jats:italic> DSM 5425<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>. However, DNA–DNA relatedness between the new isolates and the closest related <jats:italic>Halomonas</jats:italic> species was low.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>The problems associated with the salinization of soils and water bodies and the increasing competition for scarce freshwater resources are increasing. Current attempts to adapt to these conditions through sustainable agriculture involves searching for new highly salt-tolerant crops, and wild species that have potential as saline crops are particularly suitable. The common ice plant (Mesembryanthemum crystallinum L.) is an edible halophyte member of the Aizoaceae family, which switches from C3 photosynthesis to crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) when exposed to salinity or water stress. The aim of this review was to examine the potential of using the ice plant in both the wild and as a crop, and to describe its ecology and morphology, environmental and agronomic requirements, and physiology. The antioxidant properties and mineral composition of the ice plant are also beneficial to human health and have been extensively examined.</jats:p>
title: Halophyte Common Ice Plants: A Future Solution to Arable Land Salinization

abstract: <jats:p>Saline habitats cover a wide area of our planet and halophytes (plants growing naturally in saline soils) are increasingly used for human benefits. Beside their genetic and physiological adaptations to salt, complex ecological processes affect the salinity tolerance of halophytes. Hence, prokaryotes and fungi inhabiting roots and leaves can contribute significantly to plant performance. Members of the two prokaryotic domains Bacteria and Archaea, as well as of the fungal kingdom are known to be able to adapt to a range of changes in external osmolarity. Shifts in the microbial community composition with increasing soil salinity have been suggested and research in functional interactions between plants and micro-organisms contributing to salt stress tolerance is gaining interest. Among others, microbial biosynthesis of polymers, exopolysaccharides, phytohormones and phytohormones-degrading enzymes could be involved.</jats:p>
title: Properties of the halophyte microbiome and their implications for plant salt tolerance

<jats:p>
                    Protein splicing is the self‐catalyzed excision of an intervening polypeptide (intein) from flanking polypeptides (exteins), concomitant with the ligation of the extein. An intein in the archaebacterium
                    <jats:italic>Halobacterium salinarum</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic>Hsa</jats:italic>
                    ) interrupts the DNA Polymerase II. We have observed that the Hsa intein splices poorly in Escherichia coli cells, unlike two highly related inteins found in
                    <jats:italic>Pyrococcus abyssi</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>Methanoculleus marisnigri</jats:italic>
                    , which are not halophilic. To test if splicing activity depends on salinity, we altered the expression conditions by varying the salinity of the growth media and of in vitro activity assays. Future experiments will involve in vivo techniques by over‐expressing the intein and the flanking exteins into
                    <jats:italic>Hsa</jats:italic>
                    , and by using antibodies to detect possible splicing of the native protein.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:title>Summary</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Caspase‐like proteases are key initiators and executioners of programmed cell death (
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">PCD</jats:styled-content>
                    ), which is initiated by environmental stimuli and manifests in organisms ranging from unicellular microbes to higher eukaryotes.
                    <jats:italic>
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">A</jats:styled-content>
                      rchaea
                    </jats:italic>
                    had been absent from the caspase inheritance discussion due to a lack of gene homologues. We recently demonstrated extremely high, basal caspase‐like catalytic activity in the model haloarcheon,
                    <jats:italic>
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">H</jats:styled-content>
                      aloferax volcanii
                    </jats:italic>
                    , which was linked to the cellular stress response and was widespread among diverse
                    <jats:italic>
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">A</jats:styled-content>
                      rchaea
                    </jats:italic>
                    . Here, we rigorously tested the catalytic specificity of the observed archaeal caspase‐like activities using hydrolytic assays with a diverse suite of protease substrates and inhibitors compared with known model serine and cysteine proteases (trypsin, cathepsin, papain, and human caspase‐8). Our experiments demonstrate that exponentially growing
                    <jats:italic>
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">H</jats:styled-content>
                      . volcanii
                    </jats:italic>
                    possesses a highly specific caspase‐like activity that most closely resembles caspase‐4, is preferentially inhibited by the pan‐caspase inhibitor,
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">zVAD</jats:styled-content>
                    ‐
                    <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">FMK</jats:styled-content>
                    , and has no cross‐reactivity with other known protease families. Our findings firmly root the extremely high levels of caspase‐like activity as the dominant proteolytic activity in this extreme haloarcheaon, thereby providing further support for housekeeping functions in
                    <jats:italic>
                      <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">H</jats:styled-content>
                      aloarchaea
                    </jats:italic>
                    . Given the deep archaeal roots of eukaryotes, we suggest that this activity served as a foundation for stress pathways in higher organisms.
                  </jats:p>
title: Specificity of archaeal caspase activity in the extreme halophile H aloferax volcanii
